utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would the Registrar call the list, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-24-PT, Prosecutor versus Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Brenda Hollis along with Michael Keegan and Ann Sutherland appearing on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dusan Vucicevic and Anthony D'Amato on behalf of the defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can the accused hear? Can you hear, Dr. Kovacevic? Very well. The first matter to deal with is this, that I said that we would make a ruling this morning on the first Prosecution motion in relation to the protection of witnesses and also the various requests by the Defence for relief which was set out in their reply. Dealing, first of all, with the Prosecution motion, having in mind our obligation to provide for the protection of witnesses, we shall grant that motion and make the usual order. In relation to the relief sought in the Defence reply, we shall refuse that application for relief. In the case of Delalic which I mentioned yesterday, which was a decision of Trial Chamber 2 on the 18th of March last year, it was held that the Defence does not have any right to obtain information concerning Prosecution witnesses for the purpose of conducting pre-trial interviews. This Chamber endorses that decision. There is no right to conduct such interviews. No such right is reflected in Article 21 of the Statute or in Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and, as such, the conduct of interviews in these circumstances does not form part of the practice of the International Tribunal even when it is acceded to by the Prosecution. I would add this, that the Trial Chamber also considers that there is a danger that such pre-trial interviews may add further to the distress of victims and witnesses. For those reasons, this relief is denied. One further matter before we continue with the hearing of the motions, and it is this: It concerns the last motion that we were dealing with concerning the pre-trial admission of documents. Ms. Hollis, it occurs to us that Friday afternoon this week will be available for the resolution of any disputes that there may be about that matter arising from any conference between the parties later this week. It has this advantage, that fixing other times during the court calendar in the next few weeks may be difficult, whereas that time is available. So what I'm going to ask the parties to do is to discuss these issues in the next couple of days and, if necessary, if required, we will list a hearing for 2.00 p.m. on Friday. Will that be of assistance, do you think, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have already agreed with the Defence to meet with them Thursday to discuss the documents, so that a Friday hearing, if necessary, then would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if you would undertake to notify us and notify the authorities after your conference, as to whether a hearing is going to be needed, we will be available to conduct it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for your consideration of this matter. However, with the best intentions, it will not be possible for us to accomplish it because after, as you may recall, there was quite a bit of a misunderstanding on my part what was turned over to us or not, and we had made agreement to have a conference on Thursday, but then we all learned that the documents that Mr. Keegan was talking about were turned over to the Registry and the Trial Chamber, and we really didn't receive them. So I was handed a box of 1,200 pages yesterday, and I started reviewing some of them yesterday. It will not be possible, physically possible, to go through all of them, and we will have to postpone this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do what you can, Mr. Vucicevic. No doubt at least you will be able to take a view about some of the documents. If you can take a view and you can discuss the matters in conference, we will have the hearing on Friday, but if it's not possible, then it will have to be postponed. So to some extent, we are in your hands. If you think that a meeting would be profitable, a hearing would be profitable on some of the documents, we will hold it. Otherwise, we won't. But after you have had the conference, perhaps you can consider the matter with the Prosecution and decide whether a hearing would be profitable or not. If not, we will have to have a hearing at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am mindful of your suggestion and, you know, giving us, you know, this opportunity. But looking at the amount of the material that is there and taking into consideration that I only got the chance to review half of the witness statements that were sent to me, of 25 witness statements there were given before, some material also included with that material, so that we are talking maybe close to 2,000 pages. Combined with that, my back is not doing fine, you know, because I kind of, you know, my back started acting up on me when I flew over here from Chicago, so I'm not sure how much physically I will be able to accomplish to Thursday, and that's why -- because I will be put into the position where it will not be that I will have to rush through those documents, that I will not be able to connect them with the other witness statements. I don't think I will do justice to my case, Your Honour, by this approach. I really need the time to digest those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you think that we can make any progress on Friday, we will hold the hearing, but it sounds very much as though we won't be able to, in which case it will have to be held at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But I would add this, that we will have a hearing on Friday only for the purpose of discussing that particular motion. We do not want to have a hearing in order to re-litigate matters which have been decided today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I am absolutely mindful of your decision and will follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato, I think that the last matter we have to deal with in open session concerns matters which you raised in your reply to the indictment which contained a request for relief. If you would like to address us on these particular matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Should I take the four of them in order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whichever order suits you.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: All right. We have four requests for relief in light of the Prosecution's brief, and I know that the Prosecution will want to reply to this, so let me make my case without repeating the arguments in the brief but just as a summary. First of all, in the indictment, it is said that Dr. Kovacevic is accused of genocide, yet Article 4 of the Statute talks about "genocide or other acts," and the indictment appears to be talking only about this "or other acts" and not about genocide at all. Under the principle, I think, which is common to every legal system in the world, indictments must be strictly and severely construed against the Prosecutor. If a person is being charged with a crime of genocide but there is nothing in the indictment that suggests that he was guilty of genocide, then it seems that the indictment is basically flawed and should be dismissed in its entirety. Second, the caption "Superior Authority" immediately following paragraph 2 of the indictment does not correspond to any legal principle that I'm aware of. It's a shorthand form. But as it stands, it seems to me that it has no place in an indictment and should be struck. Number 3, the conclusion at the end of the indictment -- let me get it -- says: "By these acts and omissions, SIMO DRLJACA and MILAN KOVACEVIC were complicit in the commission of GENOCIDE, punishable under Articles 4(3)(e) and 7(1) ... of the Statute of the Tribunal" raises in conclusory form something that should have been set out in the operative paragraphs, and there is nothing in the operative paragraph that says anything about complicity; and therefore, under the general argument that it should be severely construed against the Prosecutor, that part of it should be struck. And secondly, Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute are being raised here for the first time in a conclusory sentence without any supporting authority, without any reference to what it might be in the indictment that corresponds to Articles 7(1) and 7(3). And, to boot the entire Prosecution's pre-trial brief never mentions Article 7(1) and 7(3). If it's an afterthought, an afterthought should not be the sort of thing that should send a person to prison for the rest of his life, and again, this ought to be struck as well. Finally, number 4, the last conference that we had, Your Honours, there was a suggestion that many of these pre-trial motions ought to be done in the spirit of narrowing the issues so the trial can proceed economically. The Prosecution's gloss, however, on the notion of genocide broadens it to the point where it can include everything. Apparently, under the Prosecution's brief -- and I went into this in great detail so I'm only summarising right now -- but under the Prosecution's brief, deportation is an act of genocide, persecution is an act of genocide. Well, if you can allow that to happen as an expansion of the concept, what we're going to see at the trial are all kinds of testimony about deportation and persecution and many other things that are really not at all relevant, they're not acts of genocide, they're not acts under Article 4 of the Statute, they have never been considered to be acts of genocide except in some dicta that the Prosecution cites, and of course I went into that in the brief and said that that dicta doesn't have any legal compulsion. So under the principle that the pre-trial brief should be focusing and narrowing the issues, it's my contention that the Prosecution, for its own reasons, deliberately broadened the concept so that the trial can just about include everything, and it would seem to me that rather than having to argue this issue every time a witness comes up, we get into the exact same argument that we are going through today, namely, that this witness's testimony might be relevant to persecution or it might be relevant to deportation but it's not relevant to genocide and the Prosecution comes back and they cite the Eichmann case and then we go into that, we would have to do that 100 times. I think in terms of efficiency, we should adopt pre-trial the definition of genocide that is common that everybody accepts and that is not full of this gloss that expands it to the point where everything is allowed in. And my suggestion to the Court is to simply take the 140 words of Article 4 and say that is the accepted definition of genocide. Of course, that includes the meaning of those words, how they -- the Traveaux preparatoirs -- all the things that had to do with how those words came to be, that's fine, but not to add on top of it a disposition and a treatise on genocide broadly defined as the Prosecution did because I think that will make the trial almost impossible to conduct, it will be nothing but a bunch of repetitious legal arguments every step of the way. So my suggestion on this fourth is to confine the operative legal principle of the trial to the exact words of the Statute to which, of course, we have no dispute whatsoever. Your Honours, I could say a little bit more, but I would like to reserve one or two minutes in the event the Prosecution -- in the event of a possible rebuttal. Would that be possible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In looking at the Defence response to the pre-trial brief, we would suggest, first of all, that the Defence response goes well beyond a response to the pre-trial brief, and, in effect, what it does is, in the body of what is purported to be a response, raises two different motions, hence leading to a conclusion in their supposed response that actually includes requests for relief. We do not typically look at a response to a pre-trial brief to include requests for relief. So indeed, once again, we have embodied in a response what we consider to be really two independent motions for relief. Perhaps in the future as a term of practice it would be better to set out motions independently. Nevertheless, we suggest that's what we have here. Within the response, we have two motions for relief. The first motion is to strike portions of the indictment, and in that regard, the Defence talks about superior authority and then talks about the language following paragraph 16. If we look a bit at the history of this case, it will lead us to the conclusion that this motion to strike portions of the indictment should not be allowed for a variety of reasons. This motion, a motion to strike portions of the indictment, was first raised in a written pleading by the Defence in September of 1997, and the Prosecution filed a written response on 24 September of 1997. The Trial Chamber to which this case was assigned at that time is not the current Trial Chamber, and that Trial Chamber did not hear and dispose of this motion. However, during a motions hearing before this Trial Chamber in February of this year, the Defence, in fact, withdrew or dropped this motion to strike portions of the indictment. They dropped it. Now they're trying to resurrect it. They should not be allowed such a fragmented approach to this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just help us? You're quite right about that because I remember the occasion. What was the nature of that motion? I think the -- the point of superior authority was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It included superior authority, it included a concern about what was in the background material, and I believe at that time in the motion that was filed in September, they also asked that references to Simo Drljaca be stricken. The Prosecution in its reply to that indicated we would do so and, in fact, as a housekeeping matter we have complied with that and we do now have an indictment from which the references to Simo Drljaca have been stricken and we will provide that to the Trial Chamber and the Defence for their review. So that was what was included in their motion to strike. If there were other concerns they had with the indictment, they should have included them in that motion to strike. Nonetheless, in February, they, in fact, withdrew that motion. They said they wanted to drop the matter. And now they're resurrecting it again. On that basis alone we would suggest you should deny this motion and this fragmented approach to motions practice. That point aside, if we look at what they are now asking, we look at, first of all, their complaint about the caption "Superior Authority," and we suggest that their complaint concerning that caption has no basis in the Statute of this tribunal. First of all, Article 7(3) speaks in terms of a superior, a superior and a subordinate, and if we want to clarify what is meant by 7(3) we simply have to look at paragraph 56 of the Secretary-General's report concerning the creation of this Tribunal, and in paragraph 56, which is certainly available to the Defence, the Secretary-General speaks in terms of "Superior Authority." Therefore, we would suggest this is not surplusage, it is a way to focus in on the paragraphs that follow "Superior Authority", and we're talking in terms of 7(3), which is one of the bases on which an accused may be held individually criminally liable for acts or omissions. If we look at paragraph 13 of the Defence response wherein they ask the Trial Chamber to strike the language that follows paragraph 16 of our indictment, first, as stated before, they shouldn't be allowed to have such a fragmented approach to a motion but, in fact, this Trial Chamber should consider this matter to be waived by their February withdrawal of the motion. Beyond that, the requested relief is certainly not warranted. The language following paragraph 16 sets forth the charge in the case, complicity and genocide, 4(3)(e) under the Statute. Secondly it sets forth the basis for individual criminal liability. In this case, the Prosecution is alleging this accused is individually criminally liable pursuant both to Article 7(1) and Article 7(3). In addition, when we look at the language that the acts and omissions form the basis for this liability, both individual criminal liability and genocide under the Statute, the acts and omissions referred to are the paragraphs which precede this language. They are the enumerated paragraphs above. This is not surplusage, this does not introduce new elements into any offence of genocide, it, in fact, sets out the particular act under subparagraph 3 of Article 4 which we are charging, and it sets out the individual criminal liability bases upon which we are proceeding. The Defence argues that these -- this motion to strike is really a response to our pre-trial brief, but, in effect, what it is, is a motion pertaining to the indictment and the form of the indictment, so it is not really responsive to the Court's order that they respond to a pre-trial brief. One motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, may I say, you're clearly right about that. If we were going to be technical about it, we could simply refuse to accept the motion or the relief application and order them to file a separate motion, and our hearing it today is merely a matter of convenience and, of course, mustn't be taken as condoning any departure from the normal practice which should be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we certainly do appreciate the convenience that is given by addressing this -- how it has been raised, and that's what we are attempting to do. In that regard, Your Honour, we would point out that because we received this very recently -- I believe it was Friday of last week -- we have not had the ability to date to file a written reply to this. Certainly because these motions are very serious motions, we would request the right to file a more complete response if the Trial Chamber believes that would be warranted. But moving on, Your Honour, to the second motion that they attempt to raise in their response. This appears to be a motion alleging defects in the form of the indictment, and in reviewing this again, perhaps, first of all, if we may, in a more technical sense in terms of pleadings and timing of pleadings, we would point out the following: That this accused had his initial appearance on the 30th of July of 1997. The Rules that were then in effect gave the accused 60 days from his initial appearance to file a motion such as this, a motion relating to defects in the form of the indictment. His time to have filed such a motion would have ended on the 1st of October. The Rule, our present Rule, is a different Rule. That Rule was not changed until the 20th of October and the 12th of November amendments were added to the Rules for the Tribunal. We suggest that under this reading, looking at the Rule in place at the time of the initial appearance and at the time of the running of the 60 days, that this motion is an untimely motion. Beyond that, we would suggest that again this is a fragmented approach to motions practice. The Defence obviously reviewed the indictment and they reviewed it carefully because in September they set forth their motion to strike certain portions. Why did they not at that time include a motion alleging defects in the form of the indictment? Your Honour, as I said, that is a technical matter. We will go beyond that and talk about what they are discussing in what appears to be a motion alleging defects in the form of the indictment. First of all, they refer to paragraph 9 of the indictment and assert that based on defects in that paragraph, the entire indictment should be dismissed and should be dismissed with prejudice. As part of that assertion, they assert that charging the accused -- that we're charging with the accused with genocide in paragraph 9 but that not a single one of the acts and omissions complained of in the paragraphs following paragraph 9 refer to acts of genocide as specified in Article 4(2), that is enumerated acts. On that latter assertion, Your Honour, we suggest that they are completely without foundation in the indictment. First of all, that latter assertion misperceives the required structure of an indictment. It is not required that every paragraph in an indictment be able to stand on its own as a legal charge, as a mini indictment, if you will. You must consider the indictment as a whole. And certainly, looking at the paragraphs following paragraph 9, those paragraphs are replete with assertions that constitute enumerated acts under Article 4(2). They speak of killings that occurred in the camps. Killings are specified as an enumerated act under 4(2), 4(2)(a), they speak of beatings, torture, sexual assault, and other such attacks on the persons. This is covered by the enumerated act 4(2)(b), which talks about causing serious bodily or mental harm on members of this group. They also talk about people being detained because of their ethnic or religious group. They talk about conditions of life that are calculated to bring about the physical destruction of the group. That is subparagraph 4(2)(c), so the allegation, the assertion that there are no enumerated acts asserted in the paragraphs that follow paragraph 9 is simply not true. Concerning the language of paragraph 9, should this Trial Chamber determine that by that language the Prosecution is attempting to allege another act under subparagraph 3, the appropriate action for this Trial Chamber to take would be to strike paragraph 9. It certainly would not be, for this Trial Chamber, to dismiss the indictment, because to do that you must look at the indictment as a whole, and as a whole, the indictment sets forth a basis for the charges, sets forth the charges, sets forth the basis for individual criminal liability. Furthermore, there is certainly no basis for this Trial Chamber to conclude that even were they to dismiss the indictment, they must do so with prejudice. There is no indication that we went forward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does striking or dismissing it with prejudice mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: With prejudice, I assume, Your Honour, that we would not be allowed to amend the indictment to cure the defects and go forward. That is my understanding of "with prejudice" compared to "without prejudice," and that is the position from which I am speaking, Your Honour. Of course, if the Trial Chamber has a different definition, then my remarks would not be on point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got no definition at all, so I wanted to find out what it meant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: For those reasons, Your Honour, we would suggest that this motion to dismiss the indictment or the motion alleging defects in the indictment and asking for the relief of dismissal with prejudice should be denied. Your Honour, turning to the concerns the Defence had on the pre-trial brief itself next, if I might? First of all, I would like to point out that the concerns they allege regarding this pre-trial brief seems to misapprehend the function of the pre-trial brief. The most significant function perhaps is the last function that was listed by this Court's order, and that is to identify points that are at issue. And certainly, if you read the Defence response to our pre-trial brief, you will realise the points we raised are all at issue in terms of the Defence. If we look at the Defence response as denying or agreeing to those points, you will see that in every instance where we have raised our position on a legal matter that must be decided by this Trial Chamber -- at least in the view of the Prosecution that must be decided by this Trial Chamber -- the Defence has basically said that they disagree with our position. So in that regard, we have done a very good job of identifying points in issue, and it appears that all points are in issue. And there is really no way for the Prosecution to narrow points in dispute if, in fact, all the points are in dispute. First of all, we suggest that by a plea of not guilty and by the lack of any stipulation as to any element, then the plea of not guilty and the lack of stipulation does place all the elements in dispute and, of course, the Prosecution must prove them beyond a reasonable doubt. Beyond that, in regard to the positions on the various elements and the definitions that we set forth in our pre-trial brief, it appears the Defence disagrees with all of those positions and definitions. Ultimately, this Trial Chamber will have to decide, much beyond the elements of genocide as they are set forth in Article 4, they will have to decide also the scope and the meaning of the various bases for individual criminal liability as they pertain to this case. They will have to determine -- you, the Trial Chamber, will have to determine how you define the various elements, what the parameters of those various elements of genocide are within the scope of the facts of this case. You will also have to decide what complicity means in terms of culpability within the scope of the facts of this case. Those are legal issues this Trial Chamber will have to address. When you choose to address them is entirely up to you. In the Tadic case, we requested, along with the Defence, that the Trial Chamber provide us with their elements of the offences as well as their definitions of those elements before we went to trial. The Trial Chamber indicated that that would be developed as the facts came in and that at the conclusion of the case, they would make those determinations. However this Trial Chamber may choose to decide those issues, at some point, of course, you must decide them. And the reason we put forth the points that we put forth is because the Prosecution believes those are relevant to issues you must decide. In toto then, Your Honour, regarding the request for relief that the Defence have raised through their response, we would ask that you deny these requests for relief. We would also ask, as I indicated earlier, to the extent you believe it is necessary, we be allowed to file a written response to the motions that they have raised in their response. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato, it's right, isn't it, that you did withdraw your original motion in relation at least to "Superior Authority." That's my clear recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I concede that, and I concede the point on "Superior Authority." That was covered before. I don't concede the general point that we're estopped -- we are ever estopped thereafter from raising problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not estopped, but it's rather against you if you have withdrawn it once.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: On "Superior Authority," yes, but on the other issues they say why didn't we complain about that earlier? I think if there are fatal defects in an indictment, we are never estopped from complaining. Even at trial, we could bring it up. The defendant should not be punished with life imprisonment because the attorneys weren't quick enough to point out a fatal flaw in the indictment. If the indictment is fatally flawed, even the Court itself could notice that at any point in the trial and throw the case out. So I don't think estoppel carries as far as Ms. Hollis suggested, but I certainly agree with her about -- I think we have to concede on the "Superior Authority" question. I also want to say in response briefly to the idea that we should have been bringing this up in motions and what does it have to do with their pre-trial brief, if I may remind the Court that in scheduling order of March 5th, you told us to file one or more documents setting out those points, if any, of the indictment and the Prosecution pre-trial brief, those which are admitted, those which are denied. Well, this motion -- this Defence reply that I filed on the 7th, just hours before we caught the plane to come here, is entitled "Defence reply to the indictment and to the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief." So we tried to do it in one document -- when you said one or more documents, we tried to do it all in one, and we tried to reply to the indictment as well as the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, and I think that we are following the court's directive there and not trying to do something that was outside of motion practice. I think the idea here is to try to do these things economically and get them to you in time so the Prosecution could have a few days to look at them while we are en route to The Hague. On the question of dismissing with prejudice the indictment against Dr. Kovacevic because of the allegation of genocide, I think Ms. Hollis' arguments are well-presented and give the Court an opportunity to consider the question from both sides, and I really have no comment except to say that when Ms. Hollis says that the subsequent paragraphs do refer to acts enumerated in Article 4(2), killings, for example, I respectfully disagree. The killings are only relevant to genocide if they are undertaken with the intent to destroy in whole or in part members of a group because of their membership in a group as such. And there's no allegation about that. There certainly are allegations of killings, but to connect that up to genocide is not done in the indictment where it should have been. Perhaps this issue is one, as Ms. Hollis suggests, that deserves briefing on both sides, written briefing. So we would certainly, if the Court wishes to have that, we would be delighted to engage in that activity in the next week or so, if that's what the Court wishes. I disagree with Ms. Hollis' remark that if she raises any issue in the brief and we dispute it, then it becomes relevant because it's a disputed point. I mean, under that theory, you could raise in your brief crimes against humanity, violations of the Genocide Convention, airjacking, hijacking, all kinds of things, and if we object to them suddenly they become relevant because she says now they're an issue. I mean, that to me, that is no standard of what constitutes something being an issue. With respect to the arguments about deportation and persecution and other things, our position is that's irrelevant to this trial, totally irrelevant. Ms. Hollis is suggesting that because we're saying it's irrelevant, they now become issues that are properly before the Court. A very interesting argumentative strategy, but I think the court will understand that what we are saying is they have nothing to do with this case and therefore they're not an issue. They're being introduced for the purposes of broadening the concept of genocide and creating at the trial, almost with every witness, a mini trial on the legal issues of what constitutes genocide, and I again repeat that I think the most economical way to approach is to take the common elements here, namely the words of the Statute, and proceed on that. And that's what genocide means. It doesn't mean the extensive broadening that appears in the Prosecution's brief on the question because those are just speculations and we dispute those. On the other hand, if the Court would like us to argue each one of those points separately, we are certainly prepared and willing to do that. Your Honour, I think I covered the points I want to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider this motion and we will rise for half an hour. Sit again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 11.20 a.m. (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We deal with the requests for relief by the Defence. First, the reference to "Superior Authority." That point was conceded on the 27th of February and is conceded again, so there is no need for us to make any ruling. As for the remaining matters, they all relate, in effect, to the substance of the indictment. In our judgement, they are misconceived. The indictment must be read as a whole and not by individual paragraphs. Those paragraphs are not independent of each other but must be read together. Equally, we do not accept that the Prosecution are trying to broaden the definition of "genocide" as is suggested. For instance, the references to deportation and persecution, to which Mr. D'Amato has referred, are capable, in our judgement, of coming within the definitions in Article 4(2)(b) and (c). Accordingly, these requests for relief are refused. However, we have considered the suggestion which has been made by Ms. Hollis in relation to briefs upon definition of the elements of genocide, and we have come to the conclusion that we would find it helpful to have briefs from both sides defining the legal elements of genocide. We appreciate that the Prosecution pre-trial brief, in fact, is directed to that issue, but we would invite the Prosecution to consider within 28 days and, if so advised, to expand that definition, and we would be helped by a brief from the Defence, again with 28 days. Mr. D'Amato, is there any difficulty about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No. In general, Your Honour, I just want to ask two quick questions: Will we be responding to the Prosecution's brief; in other words, what we have here we will write a brief on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: And secondly, would you consider limiting the definition of genocide to those issues that are applicable to the defendant in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we would want the matter defined in relation to this case, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Fine. So if there are things that are quite unrelated, they would not be included in the definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: An academic discourse is not needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I say, that we would find helpful. I would add this: Both parties should file copies of their authorities in English, please, with the brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: At the request of the Presiding Judge, I would like to draw your attention, when considering the various issues relating to genocide, to a recent judgement delivered by a German court in a case -- I do not remember by heart the date but I think it's the Jorgis case, J-O-R-G-I-S. I am afraid it is available only in German, but we do have a copy here in the library of our Tribunal, so it might be useful for both parties to study carefully this case because it deals with genocide in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When those briefs have been filed, the Trial Chamber will consider them and decide whether it would be appropriate or not to make any sort of ruling, but we will consider that in due course. Are there any other matters to be dealt with in open session before we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I may have the floor, Your Honours? Just two points of clarification. I had an opportunity to discuss with Mr. Keegan from the Office of the Prosecutor our conference concerning documents that are requested to be admitted and it seems, you know, practically it will be impossible to go through all of these documents that I have today and tie up the whole, you know, bunch of documents that I have in my office in Chicago that have been sent there by the Office of the Prosecutor, and I can't make any kind of agreements with him until I review all of that material, so I would respectfully ask you to postpone the conference -- the opportunity you have given us for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: That's number 1. And number 2, I hope -- I am just making this remark so hoping that this is going to come in your written decision. When you made the ruling on the protection of witnesses and to the extent to which Defence has the opportunity, as you put it, right to interview them, and, you know, I respect your decision. However, I am a little bit in an unclear situation about the points that I have not so strongly raised in my brief as far as the psychiatric evaluation of the witnesses and refugees from Bosnia. And if I may, I'm not quite sure whether your ruling is referring to disclosure of any information of the psychiatric treatments of all the witnesses that are going to be testifying and who have been subjected to this form of recovery of suppressed memory. This is extremely critical to us to evaluate these witnesses and since you have not articulated that part -- I am not asking you to do so, I am just merely emphasising the point that I did not sufficiently it emphasise in our brief. And with the University of Illinois in Chicago, there is a professor of psychiatry who has been in charge of the Hartland Institute, I believe the programme is called, who has been working for a few years with refugees from Bosnia and -- several hundreds of them, and there is a man from Kozarac whose name was in the paper and there were statements about this type of therapy. That's where the information came to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, we have made our ruling. That is, we are denying your applications. The Prosecution have said that they will ask the witnesses about these matters and inform you of any such information which they receive. Beyond that, no further interviews or requests should be made. So the answer is that your applications, your applications for relief, have been refused, and the position is you will get whatever information the Prosecution is able to give you. For the rest of the matter, you must ask the witnesses when they come to be cross-examined, but no further application to interview them can be entertained. So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, looking in the practical matters, and this is not -- this is just further clarification -- nothing, because, you know, your decision is fully accepted -- fully, you know, accepted, you know, I'm not asking you, you know, to do anything about it, because when I'm looking further down in cross-examining these witnesses, I am quite dismayed that asking a witness what had happened -- "Have you had psychiatric treatment or not?" If I have to ask every witness who come before you, I am afraid I will sound like a broken record, and after a couple of times you'll say, "Mr. Vucicevic, please don't ask that question anymore."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's worry about that when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there are no further matters for open session, the Court will go into closed session now. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 22 (status conference dealt with in another document) 23 24 25
